14. The checker

Say a reviewer asks what actually happens when you call @sv.transform. The answer is a small command-line program that does the work. The Lean project compiles to it, substrait-check. It is the bridge between the proofs and real queries: it reads a Substrait plan (as JSON), translates it into the Lean model Rel, and runs checks that are proved to answer the mathematical questions they claim to answer. sverify calls it behind the scenes for everything in the rest of the tour, and you can run it yourself.
Mode What it does Used by
substrait-check plan.json show the plan, check it is well-formed, evaluate it this chapter
--write plan.json write the plan back out from Lean's model the engines (chapter 11)
--contract contract.json prove postconditions from preconditions contracts (chapters 4–8)
--delta plan.json the proved update plans for incremental views chapters 9–10
Exit codes: 0 fine, 1 unsupported or unparseable, 2 ill-formed, 3 not incrementally maintainable, 4 a postcondition not proved.

A real plan

Let's start with some tables, registered in DataFusion, which compiles the SQL here:

sverify.engines.substrait_json asks DataFusion for the Substrait plan of a query. Edit the SQL and the checker re-runs. Try a join (select o.id, c.city from orders o join customers c on o.customer = c.name), a limit 2, or a group by (which the model doesn't cover yet).

$ substrait-check plan.json
Emit [3, 4]
  Project +[$0, ($2 * 2)]
    Filter (10 < $2)
      Read orders
tables: orders(3)
arity: 2
well-formed: yes
incremental: yes
roundtrip: ok
rows (0):

data.text/markdown:
What each line means, for the default query:
  • The tree is the plan, printed from Lean's model, root first. $2 is column 2 of the operator's input, here amount. The Project appends two columns, a copy of id ($0) and amount * 2, as columns 3 and 4, and the Emit keeps just those two.
  • tables: the tables the plan reads, with their number of columns.
  • arity: how many columns the result has.
  • well-formed: yes: every column reference exists. This is decided by Rel.checkWF, which is proved to agree with the mathematical definition Rel.WF (theorem checkWF_iff). So the type-safety theorem Rel.eval_arity applies: every output row has exactly arity columns.
  • incremental: yes: the plan can be maintained from changes alone (chapter 9). Also a decision procedure with a proof (isIncremental_iff).
  • roundtrip: ok: writing the Rel back to JSON and reading it again gives the same Rel. That guards the parser, which is trusted code (chapter 15).
  • rows (0): named tables carry only their schema here, no data.

Ruling out column bugs

Since columns are numbered, a classic bug is a reference to a column that doesn't exist. Move the slider to change which column the filter reads, by editing the plan's JSON directly:

($0 is well-formed but compares id instead of amount with 10: well-formedness rules out references to nothing, not references to the wrong thing. Catching that is what contracts are for, from chapter 4 on.)

Lean as a reference engine

Rel.eval is executable, so the checker can also run a plan, as long as the data is inside the plan. sverify.testing.inline_tables replaces each table read by a Substrait VALUES list, and lean_rows runs that plan through Rel.eval. This is how the test suite compares the engines against the Lean semantics, the definition of correct. Here is your query from above, run by Lean and by DataFusion on the same rows:

Writing plans back out

--write prints the plan as Lean understood it, as Substrait JSON produced from the Rel (sverify.engines.written_plan in Python). How much of Ibis gets through

Not every query fits the Lean model yet. sverify.coverage compiles a list of Ibis operations and hands each to the checker: ✓ means it is verified (so contracts apply), ✗ that the checker refuses it, – that Ibis or DataFusion fails before there is a plan, and inc. that it can also be maintained incrementally. Refusing is the safe default: a plan outside the model is never checked against the wrong semantics.
